article_text:
20世紀オランダを代表する版画家・グラフィックアーティストの マウリッツ・コルネリス・エッシャー （M.C.エッシャー）の創造の軌跡をたどる展覧会 「エッシャー 無限のつくりかた」 が、2027年7月2日から9月26日まで CREATIVE MUSEUM TOKYO で開催される。

本展では、M.C.エッシャー財団が所蔵する膨大なコレクションから、代表作を含む約200点を展示。木版画やリトグラフによる幾何学的な反復パターン、錯視、不可能な建築、イメージの変容など、エッシャーの作品を特徴づける代表的なテーマを紹介する。

会場では、初期の作品からイタリア滞在中に描いた風景や建築、スペインのアルハンブラ宮殿の装飾文様に着想を得て発展させた「平面充填」まで、創作の変遷をたどる。さらに、数学や幾何学への関心を背景に生み出された「無限」や「不可能空間」などの作品も取り上げる。卓越した版画技術と知的な探求心が融合したエッシャーの表現を、作品だけでなく、その思考の源泉にも着目しながらひもとく内容となる。

エッシャーは1898年にオランダで生まれ、ハールレムの建築・装飾芸術・工芸学校で学んだ。教師サミュエル・イェッセリュン・デ・メスキータの勧めをきっかけに版画芸術に取り組み、1920年代から1930年代にかけてイタリアに滞在。風景や建築を描く一方、スペインのアルハンブラ宮殿を訪れ、装飾文様から強い刺激を受けた。とくに1936年の再訪を機に、平面充填の表現を発展させ、数学や幾何学への関心を取り入れながら、独自の作品世界を築いていった。1972年に73歳で没した後も、その作品は美術のみならず数学や建築、デザインなど幅広い分野に影響を与え続けている。

東京展終了後は、10月9日から12月8日まで、大阪の あべのハルカス美術館 に巡回する。2028年には、名古屋、静岡での開催も予定されている。

article_text:
Before the South, there was New York. And before the portraits, the vast emptiness of its architectural structures. Born in 1951, Baldwin Lee grew up in Manhattan’s Chinatown. He first studied under Minor White, a presiding figure of contemplative photography, at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, before going on to Yale, where Walker Evans’s teaching — Evans being the undisputed reference of American documentary photography — completed the formation of his eye. “I would tell my students that my photography teachers, White and Evans, were the equivalent of having studied with Matisse and Cézanne,” he recalls in an interview with Jessica Bell Brown published in Baldwin Lee (Hunters Point Press, 2022).

After graduating in 1975, he returned again and again to the city of his childhood, a 4×5 view camera on a tripod over his shoulder, moving through Manhattan at dawn, often in winter, when the sidewalks emptied of their inhabitants. “My trips to New York City from New England were an exploration of buildings as organic forms,” the artist confides. “Rather than approaching the work as architectural photography, I saw it as a way of capturing a landscape. It was my first time using a large-format camera. Early in the morning, with no one around, I felt an overwhelming intimacy — as if I were walking through my own private garden.”

His subjects include Wall Street at dawn, Times Square, and the streets and vacant lots of Lower Manhattan where the World Trade Center looms in the distance. Baldwin Lee records a city suspended between neglect and ambition, where remnants of the past remain visible alongside the structures of the new. Worn brick facades, Cadillac Eldorados parked along the curb, the twin towers still new: these images carry the trace of a human presence temporarily absent but not gone. “If the buildings were people it would be acceptable if they did not speak,” he tells Blind. “The silence can be a metaphor for spaces, once occupied, now vacant. The lack of people points to an unfulfilled potential.”

Baldwin Lee went on to teach at Yale, then at the Massachusetts College of Art. In 1982, he moved to Knoxville, Tennessee, where he founded the photography program at the university, which he would lead for more than thirty years. The following year, he embarked on an extensive series of journeys through the American South. Between 1983 and 1989, he made nearly ten thousand photographs, principally of Black communities — a body of work celebrated as a major social testament to rural Black America. “The photographs I made in the South would never have come about without adequate education and awareness: North/South, Black/white, male/female, private/public, poor/rich, powerful/subjugated,” he tells Jessica Bell Brown.

The New York photographs reveal a different but related aspect of Baldwin Lee’s practice. Their careful organization of architectural space and sustained attention to the character of place helped establish the distinctive visual language he would carry into his later work. They demonstrate a sensitivity to form and order, but also to the humanity inscribed in the built environment. His vision of New York is a record of what people made, inhabited, altered, and left behind.

The prints selected for the exhibition present his images at a scale he has never seen before. “No, I have not seen them printed at that scale,” he confides to Blind. “At this large scale the photographs and the viewer have a different relationship. A dialog between the photograph is possible and encouraged. The viewer is now capable of entering the space of the photo making for a more intimate experience.”

The twin towers that dominate several of his images have since vanished from the New York sky. The city Baldwin Lee once photographed as his own private garden no longer exists.

“Baldwin Lee: New York (1975–1979)” is on show at the Howard Greenberg Gallery from September 18, 2026 to October 31, 2026.

A reception with the artist will be held at the Howard Greenberg Gallery on Thursday, September 17, 2026 from 5:00 to 7:00 p.m.

Baldwin Lee is published by Hunters Point Press (2022).

"怀抱着年轻时的记忆，终生未曾失去独特的诗意与纯粹目光的茂田井武。以及离开忙碌日常便展开速写本、清新捕捉信州与欧洲风光的岩崎千弘。两位画家通过旅行凝视的风景与人们的身影，超越时代，至今仍在我们心底深处温柔地诉说。不妨在展厅中，伴随着同时代在巴黎绽放的艺术家们的竞演，尽情体味由旅行轨迹交织而成的无可替代的抒情吧。（美术展Navi）", "translated": true}]

article_text:
ちひろ美術館・東京（東京都練馬区）で、「没後70年 茂田井武とパリの画家たち―Parisの 破片 ―」が10月30日から開催されます。

第二次世界大戦後、子どもの本で活躍した画家・茂田井武（1908-1956）。友人から「ボヘミアン」と呼ばれた茂田井の絵には純粋な魂が息づき、忘れかけていた懐かしい感覚を呼び覚まします。1930年、21歳の茂田井は、単身パリへ渡ります。日中は給仕などをして働き、寝泊まりする安アパートに戻ると、記憶をもとにした絵を夜ごと画帳に描きためていきました。3年に渡る欧州放浪の旅で目にした各地の光景は、茂田井の心に深く刻まれ、その後も繰り返し画題となりました。

没後70年を記念した本展では、欧州滞在中の画帳「ton paris」「Parisの破片」「続・白い十字架」を中心に、パブロ・ピカソやモーリス・ユトリロ、マリー・ローランサン、藤田嗣治、板倉鼎ら当時のパリで活躍した画家たちの作品もあわせて紹介されます。さらに、帰国後に制作された画帳やタブロー、絵本、エッセイなども展示され、茂田井の創作を支え続けた大切な旅の記憶を浮かび上がらせます。

また、本展と同時期に、展示室3・4では「ちひろ 旅のたのしみ」も開催されます。本展では、国内外の風景が描かれたスケッチブックや写真を通して、ちひろの旅の思い出に光が当てられます。

没後70年 茂田井武とパリの画家たち―Parisの 破片 ― ＜同時開催＞ちひろ 旅のたのしみ

会場：ちひろ美術館・東京（東京都練馬区下石神井4-7-2）

会期：2026年10月30日（金）～2027年1月31日（日） ※会期は予告なく変更になる場合あり

開館時間：10:00～17:00（入館は閉館の30分前まで）

休館日：月曜日（祝休日は開館、翌平日休館）、年末年始（12/28～01/02）

入館料：大人1200円／高校生・18歳以下無料／65歳以上、学生の方は900円 ※障害者手帳ご提示の方とその介添えの方（1名）は無料 ※年間パスポート3000円

交通： 【電車】 西武新宿線上井草駅下車徒歩7分 【バス】 JR中央線荻窪駅より西武バス石神井公園駅行き（荻14）上井草駅入口下車徒歩5分 西武池袋線石神井公園駅より西武バス荻窪駅行き（荻14）上井草駅入口下車徒歩5分

詳細は、 ちひろ美術館・東京公式サイト まで。

展覧会の見どころ

渡欧時の3冊の画帳を一堂に「ton paris」「Parisの破片」「続・白い十字架」

1930年代のパリの街並みを瑞々しく描いた「ton paris」、異国の地での人間関係や私生活のようすが窺える「Parisの破片」、そしてスイス・ジュネーブ滞在の日々を描いた「続・白い十字架」。茂田井が欧州滞在中に描いた画帳のうち、現存する3冊が一堂に展示されます。

1920-30年代にパリに集った画家たち

ふたつの大戦に挟まれた1920年代から1930年代にかけて、芸術の都・パリには多くの画家が集いました。本展では、マリー・ローランサンやパブロ・ピカソ、モーリス・ユトリロ、板倉鼎ら、茂田井と同時代にパリで活躍した画家たちの作品も紹介されます。

欧州放浪の記憶

欧州を放浪した経験は、茂田井にとって貴重なイメージの源泉となり続けました。本展では、帰国後、旅の記憶を反芻するように制作された『古い旅の絵本』のほか、タブローや、エッセイなどが展示されます。

世界の子どもたちへ

三人の子の父親だった茂田井は、戦後の混乱のなか、児童雑誌や絵本の制作に力を注ぎました。そこには、世界の子どもたちと地球全体のしあわせを願った茂田井の切実な思いが込められています。本展では、茂田井が幼い長女のために手づくりした絵本『巴里の子供』のほか、晩年に病をおして取り組んだ、絵雑誌「キンダーブック」の仕事が掘り下げられます。

茂田井 武 プロフィール

東京に生まれる。日本橋の旅館であった生家が1923年関東大震災で全焼する。中学卒業後、太平洋画会研究所、川端画学校などで絵を学び、アテネ・フランセに通う。1930年シベリア鉄道で渡仏、1933年に帰国。職を転々とした後、探偵小説雑誌「新青年」などに挿し絵を描き、1941年から絵本を手がける。1946年日本童画会入会。戦後日本の復興期に絵本、絵雑誌などの仕事で活躍する。1954年小学館絵画賞受賞。48歳で亡くなるまで、病床で絵を描き続けた。主な絵本に『セロひきのゴーシュ』（1956）などがある。

同時開催「ちひろ 旅のたのしみ」（展示室３・４）

「没後70年 茂田井武とパリの画家たち―Parisの破片―」と同時期に開催される「ちひろ 旅のたのしみ」（展示室3・4）にも要注目です。

旅は、いわさきちひろにとって欠かせない楽しみでした。両親の郷里である信州で休暇を過ごしたり、女学校の学友たちと登山に行ったりと、幼いときから旅に親しんでいたちひろは、画業と主婦業で忙しいなかでも、時間を見つけては旅に出ました。

いつも携えていたスケッチブックには、美しい景色や、慌ただしい生活を離れゆっくり向き合った家族の姿など、旅先での感動が記されています。アルバムには、撮った場所や日付が、ちひろ自身の字で細やかに書き添えられた写真も遺されています。

本展では、国内各地やヨーロッパの旅のスケッチや写真とともに、絵本『あかいふうせん』など旅の実感をもって描かれた作品が紹介され、ちひろの旅の思い出に焦点が当てられます。

「ちひろ 旅のたのしみ」の見どころ

スケッチで楽しむ日本の秋と冬

風にそよぐすすき、鮮やかな柿の実、木枯らしに舞う葉、雪景色………。秋から冬にかけて、野山は豊かな表情を見せます。ちひろがとらえた季節の移ろいを楽しむことができます。

信州探訪―ちひろの心のふるさと

ちひろは信州を「心のふるさと」とよび、折に触れて足を運んでいました。スキー旅行や温泉旅行といった、山国ならではの旅の記録も多くあります。ちひろの信州での過ごし方や、作品に詰まった信州の魅力が紹介されます。

憧れのヨーロッパを訪ねて

1966年、ちひろは約1ヵ月をかけて、童話作家アンデルセンの故郷オーデンセをはじめパリ、ローマなどヨーロッパの都市を巡りました。200点にのぼるスケッチが現存するこの旅は、制作活動の大きな刺激となりました。パリの風情に満ちた絵本『あかいふうせん』（偕成社、1968年）を中心に、帰国後の作品もピエゾグラフで展示されます。

若き日の記憶を抱きしめ、独自の詩情と純粋なまなざしを生涯失わなかった茂田井武。そして、忙しない日常を離れてはスケッチブックを広げ、信州やヨーロッパの光景をみずみずしく捉えたいわさきちひろ。ふたりの画家が旅を通して見つめた風景や人々の姿は、時代を超えていまも私たちの心の奥深くにやさしく語りかけてきます。同時代のパリで花開いた芸術家たちの競演とともに、旅の軌跡が織りなすかけがえのない抒情を、展示室で心ゆくまで味わってみてはいかがでしょうか。（美術展ナビ）

article_text:
ビックリするほど当たるためIMA御用達の占い師・マコが、12星座の今をタロット1枚で運気予報！フォトグラファー清水はるみによるファンタスティックな星座＆大アルカナのヴィジュアルと共に、明るい未来の指針を毎月前・後半でお届けします。

10月前半に思うこと

「床を拭いて運気を2トーン上げる魔法」

10月に入り、秋風が心地よく部屋を吹き抜ける季節になりました。今回のテーマは「お掃除で開運」です！

​我が家にも文明の利器「掃除ロボット」が鎮座しておりますが、秋の運気を一気にブーストさせたい時に私が絶対に譲れない儀式。それは「手作業の雑巾がけ」です。

​便利家電も最高ですが、自分の手で四つん 這いになって床を丁寧に拭き上げると、嘘みたいにその空間が途端に2トーン明るくなった気がするから不思議！​特に力が入るのが、全ての運気がなだれ込んでくる玄関です。

​ここで登場するのが、前回ご紹介したあの最強アイテム。そう、レモンとローズマリーを煮出した特製ハーブ液！そこに塩を勢いよくぶち込んで（ここ大事！）雑巾を絞り、一心不乱に玄関のたたきを拭き上げるのです。

​邪気を弾き飛ばすレモン、トラウマや停滞感を断ち切るローズマリー、そして強力な祓いパワーを持つ塩。この「開運・三種の神器」をしみ込ませた雑巾で磨き上げると、玄関に溜まった澱んだ気が一瞬で吹き飛び、空間の密度が変わるのを肌で感じます。

​仕上げのポイントはしっかり乾拭きすること！水分を残さないことで、ツヤと良い気がバチッと定着します。

​占いでも運は足元から入ると言いますが、床や玄関を磨くことは、自分自身の土台を整えることそのもの。

​秋の夜長、お気に入りのハーブ塩水で玄関を磨き上げて、明るくなったお家で最高にツイてる秋を迎えに行きませんか？

うお座（2/19 – 3/20）

野原魔子｜Nohara Mako 東京在住。40代で突然占い師になった波乱万丈占い師。 人生に行き詰まった時、誰にも話せない事を語れたのはタロットカードでした。タロットカードは人生の設計図です。未来はこれからやって来る、良きものならそのままで、良くなきものなら明るく豊かな未来へと変えていくお手伝いをしております。人生なんとかなる！をモットーに全国駆け巡って元気をお届けします。

editorial_title_zh: 【预览】“陶瓷日本 战后日本的陶瓷设计”岐阜县现代陶艺美术馆10月24日起举办 纵览贴近日常的产业与实用陶瓷名作

article_text:
岐阜県現代陶芸美術館（岐阜県多治見市）で、「セラミックス・ジャパン 戦後日本の陶磁デザイン」が10月24日から開催されます。

戦後日本の陶磁器産業は、戦前から培われてきた技術革新やデザイン研究を基盤に、復興期を経て、1950～60年代に大きく発展しました。本展では、戦後直後に始まった実験的な試みを起点に、社会や生活文化の変化とともに展開した、戦後日本の陶磁デザインの流れに焦点が当てられます。

各地の試験場では、素材や成形技術の研究に加え、新しい生活に対応した製品やデザインの開発が進められました。また、海外のデザインや、来日した外国人専門家からの刺激も加わり、戦後の暮らしに寄り添う多様な陶磁デザインが生み出されていきます。高度経済成長期には、住まいの洋風化やLDK型の住居の普及など、暮らしのあり方が大きく変化しました。それにともない、陶磁器にも新たな需要が生まれ、さまざまなデザインの提案が試みられます。

主要産地やメーカーにおけるデザインや技術革新の動向、さらに1990年代以降に広がった手仕事やクラフトへの関心など、時代ごとの潮流にも目を向けながら、現在へと続く日本の多様な陶磁デザインの展開が紹介されます。

セラミックス・ジャパン 戦後日本の陶磁デザイン

会場：岐阜県現代陶芸美術館 ギャラリー1 （岐阜県多治見市東町4-2-5 セラミックパークMINO内）

会期：2026年10月24日（土）～2027年1月17日（日）

開館時間：10:00～18:00（入館は17:30まで）

休館日：月曜日（ただし、11/23［月・祝］、1/11［月・祝］は開館）、11/24［火］、1/12［火］、年末年始（12/28［月］～1/4［月］）

観覧料：一般1,000円、大学生800円、高校生以下および18歳未満は無料 ※身体障害者手帳、精神障害者保健福祉手帳、療育手帳、特定医療費（指定難病）受給者証・登録者証をお持ちの方および付き添いの方1名まで無料

アクセス： JR多治見駅より路線バスまたはタクシーで約10分 中央自動車道多治見インターから車で約10分

詳細は、 岐阜県現代陶芸美術館公式サイト まで。

展覧会の見どころ

戦後81年、日本の陶磁デザインの歩みをたどる

私たちの身近にある陶磁デザインは、さまざまな社会的要因に影響されながら、多様に展開してきました。本展では、これまでまとまった形で紹介されることの少なかった、日本の産業・実用陶磁器のデザインに焦点が当てられます。芸術としての「陶芸」だけではない、陶磁デザインの多様な展開に注目することができます。

柳宗理、剣持勇ら、デザイナーによる陶磁の世界

陶芸家のみならず、デザイナーや建築家、美術家たちが陶磁という素材とどのように向き合ったのかに注目します。柳宗理や剣持勇といった日本を代表するデザイナー、そして岡本太郎やイサム・ノグチといった芸術家らによる作品は、陶磁がいかにモダンデザインや建築と結びつき、展開していたのかを伝えてくれます。

メーカー、試験場、産地が支えた暮らしのデザインにふれる

戦後の陶磁器産業を支えた公設試験場や研究機関、メーカー、商社、産地の取り組みにも光が当てられます。たとえば海外市場を見据えた製品開発や海外デザインの受容、地域的な技術を活かしたデザイン、また変化するライフスタイルへ応じた提案など、それぞれの立場から生み出された、創意工夫あふれる多彩な陶磁デザインが紹介されます。

日々の食卓やリビングで何気なく手に取っている器の数々には、時代ごとの生活様式の変化や作り手たちの飽くなき探求の軌跡が息づいています。本展は、名だたるデザイナーと職人たちが挑んだ創意工夫に触れ、暮らしを彩ってきた実用陶磁器の美しさと機能美を再発見できる絶好の機会です。ぜひ会場へ足を運び、現在へと受け継がれる豊かな日本の陶磁デザインの魅力を体感してみてはいかがでしょうか。（美術展ナビ）

article_text:
Marking the awards season kickoff, a starry crowd of filmmakers and talent including Jack O’Connell and Danny Boyle (“Ink”), Sandra Hüller (“Rose”), Taron Egerton (“Everybody Wants to F*ck Me”), Rosalind Eleazer (“Misty Green”), Billie Piper (“Elsinore”), Gemma Chan (“Josephine”) and Florian Zeller (“Bunker”) turned up at Variety ‘s intimate yet glamorous dinner at Soho Mews House to celebrate the BFI London Film Festival .

The evening marked Variety ’s first London dinner, hosted by international editor Elsa Keslassy alongside London-based colleagues Alex Ritman and Ellise Shafer, in collaboration with Studiocanal.

Related Stories

'NAZA' Producer James Wilson Says Israeli Government Response to Gaza Doc Has Been ‘Horrible and Scary,’ but Directors are ‘Safe and OK’

'NAZA' Rebuttal Doc Surfaces Online, Made by IDF Reserve Members

The European powerhouse, which is part of the London-listed Canal+ Group, was out in force at the event with some hot talent from the highlights of their fall festival slate at Venice, Toronto and Telluride, as well as LFF. These included Venice opener “Ink” director Boyle, who was joined by writer James Graham and star O’Connell; LFF opener “Elsinore” writer Stephen Beresford and singer-turned-actor Piper; Zeller with “Bunker” starring Penelope Cruz and Javier Bardem; as well as “Everybody Wants To F*ck Me” director Jonathan Schey and his key cast Egerton and Mia McKenna-Bruce. Studiocanal chairman Anna Marsh, who traveled from Paris for the occasion, was there with Ron Halpern, EVP of global production, and Joe Naftalin, SVP of production and development.

Popular on Variety

Hüller, dressed in a silky red dress, also attended with “Rose” director Markus Schleinzer. Besides “Rose,” the German star is at LFF with Pawel Pawlikowski’s “Fatherland,” which could land her a pair of best actress nominations. Also in attendance were Eleazar, whose first leading role in Chris Rock’s “Misty Green” has earned some strong Oscar buzz; Chan, who stars opposite Channing Tatum in the Sundance highlight “Josephine”; and MacKay, who is currently shooting the “Ocean’s Eleven” prequel in France and presented Calvin Demba’s “The Animals” at LFF.

The gathering also drew a mix of rising talents and filmmakers, including “The Outrun” director Nora Fingscheidt; Olivia Washington, who starred in the West End production of Jeremy O. Harris’ “Slave Play”; and Savanah Leaf, who made her feature directing debut with “Earth Mama.”

The guest list reflected the breadth of the British and international film industry, with Mubi founder Efe Cakarel, whose company’s fall slate includes “Rose” and “Fatherland” as well as France’s Oscar candidate “Minotaur;” and prominent producers including Katie Goodson of Searchlight Pictures, who produced “Wild Horse Nine”; Ed Guiney and Andrew Lowe of Element Pictures; Graham Broadbent and Pete Czernin of Blueprint Pictures; Rosie Alison of Heyday; Ed Macdonald of Plan B Europe; Ben Browning of Pathé UK; Tanya Qureshi of LuckyChap International; and independent producer Rosa Attab at January Films; as well as Paris-based entertainment attorney Elsa Huisman, Independent Talent Group’s CEO Sally Long-Innes, BFI’s well-respected CEO Ben Roberts and senior production and development executive Ama Ampadu. London Film Festival artistic director Kristy Matheson, who is on her fourth year at the helm of the fest, also joined the dinner after the presentation of Andrew Haigh’s “A Long Winter.”

After a lively cocktail reception in the warmly lit lounge decorated with vintage furniture, guests sat down for a four-course dinner around two long tables dressed in white linen and softly lit by small lamps. The menu included smoked salmon with buckwheat blinis, burrata with black figs, Suffolk chicken and baked potato gnocchi, followed by desserts including sticky toffee pudding and dark chocolate mousse.

In a short speech welcoming guests, Keslassy highlighted the importance of bringing the international film community together at a time of upheaval and consolidation within the industry.

“We’re here to celebrate the London Film Festival, but also to celebrate you — filmmakers, talent, producers and executives who all have one thing in common: a desire to make movies that are not just entertaining but also bold and meaningful,” Keslassy said. “This event is meant to bring this community together, and reflect how vibrant and diverse it is.”

The evening also celebrated the close ties between the French and British film industries, with Studiocanal’s strong presence at the festival illustrating the growing crossover between talent, producers and financing partners on both sides of the Channel.

“The French and British may be the biggest rivals in many fields — including in soccer — but when it comes to cinema, we’re the best of allies!” Keslassy said.

article_text:
Netflix ‘s film VP Doug Belgrad has been let go amid a massive restructuring at the streamer.

Netflix is laying off around 1,000 employees , around 6% of its workforce, in what marks the company’s largest axing to date. Most of the cuts will effect employees on the product, technology, legal and HR teams, co-CEOs Ted Sarandos and Greg Peters told the staff on Wednesday morning.

Sheroum Kim, who served as Netflix’s director of film and worked on lower-budgeted releases like Sunny Sandler’s “Don’t Say Good Luck,” has also been let go, Variety has confirmed.

Netflix declined to comment.

“Decisions like these are never easy, and we don’t take them lightly. Our top priority today is to support those who are leaving Netflix,” the co-CEOs said in the memo, which didn’t name any of the departing employees. “The process will vary somewhat by country, but leaders will be connecting with impacted employees soon. If you are leaving, please know that we will support you throughout this transition and make sure you have as much clarity and context as possible. We also want to say thank you. What you’ve built, and the care you brought to Netflix, have made a lasting difference and we will always be grateful.”

Belgrad was hired in May 2024 and marked the first major executive appointment by film chairman Dan Lin after he succeeded Scott Stuber. Belgrad was responsible for managing Netflix’s slate of originals, including Ben Affleck’s recent crime thriller “Animals,” Affleck and Matt Damon’s “The Rip,” Adam Sandler’s “Happy Gilmore 2” and “Grown Ups 3,” the Sally Fields-led adaptation “Remarkably Bright Creatures” and “War Machine” with Alan Ritchson and Dennis Quaid.

Before joining the streamer, Belgrad was an executive at Sony for over 25 years and rose to the title of president of the Sony Pictures Entertainment Motion Picture Group. Belgrad remains chairman of 2.0 Entertainment, which is an active producer on projects such as “Unabomber” and “The Pope’s Exorcist” sequel and co-financier with Sony and Paramount on movies like “Heart of the Beast,” Primate,” “Children of Blood and Bone.”

Netflix’s last major layoffs were in 2022, when about 450 staffers were let go after a rough quarter at the streamer. Earlier this year, the company pink slipped several dozen members of its global product team .

article_text:
The 1-54 Contemporary African Art Fair has returned to London for its 14th edition, which has introduced a new section this year focused on African modernism, curated by art historian Nancy Dantas. Titled “West Wind” and inspired by Miriam Makeba’s 1966 anthem for unity, this presentation addresses the gap left by Sotheby’s when it closed its dedicated African modernism department in 2025. The showcase features mid-20th-century masters, like Ibrahim El-Salahi, Bertina Lopes, and Seyni Awa Camara, celebrating a vibrant period of political and aesthetic liberation across the continent and its diaspora. With this, the fair looks to the future while also honoring the past, illuminating the continent’s rich cultural and artistic landscape.

Below, a look at the 10 best booths at 1-54 London, which runs through Sunday at Somerset House.

Ekene Emeka Maduka at Fabienne Levy Image Credit: Emi Eleode for ARTnews Fabienne Levy presents seven paintings by Nigerian-born artist Ekene Emeka Maduka, who constructs a nostalgic “memory palace” rooted in her formative years at a Nigerian boarding school, as seen in the oil-on-canvas diptych Presence, Half-remembered (2026), showing three schoolgirls. Developed during a residency in Switzerland, these works serve as a microcosm of society, exploring themes of identity and displacement, and mark her artistic growth across Nigeria, Canada, and Switzerland. Rather than offering a direct autobiography, Maduka’s canvases immerse viewers in her subjects’ memories. The presentation contrasts the human figure with the architecture of a postcolonial modernist compound, positioning the school itself as a central protagonist. By juxtaposing Western literary influences such as William Golding’s Lord of the Flies with Chinua Achebe’s Things Fall Apart , Maduka examines the alienating frameworks of neo-colonized education and discipline. The resulting dreamscapes carry a haunting quality that lingers, capturing how context-rich environments endure in the human psyche.

Holly Rollins at Gillian Jason Gallery Image Credit: Emi Eleode for ARTnews London-based artist, designer, and interior architect Holly Rollins explores the domestic space as an archive of cultural memory and diasporic knowledge. Her exhibition comprises four sets of works, including lamps, clay photo frames, and two chairs that blur the line between functional sculpture and fine art. At the center of the display is the pink-colored Kaymito Chair (2026), made from 3D-printed recycled plastic. Working under her studio ROLSTUDIO, Rollins reinterprets familiar household forms to stimulate care, intimacy, and intergenerational memory, drawing from Caribbean matrifocal family structures. A key aspect of her philosophy is material experimentation. She combines diverse media, such as clay and memory foam, with modular systems, as seen in her custom lighting pieces positioned on a glass table and pouffe stool. Rollins’s academic research into neuro-architecture and how spatial environments influence identity informs her creation of interactive objects. Ultimately, her layout turns the booth into a landscape where everyday design elements become tangible vessels of inheritance and belonging.

Damilola Opedun at Yenwa Gallery Image Credit: Emi Eleode for ARTnews At Yenwa Gallery’s booth, two paintings, The Sacred Between and The Center Between The Noise (both 2026), tell the story of a largely forgotten community. Damilola Opedunhighlights Makoko, a vulnerable waterfront community in Lagos, creating a visual dialogue with Venice’s historic canals. The paintings also document the devastating 2025 government demolitions and land reclamation projects that have displaced Makoko residents. Opedun’s multilayered oil paintings ask whether Makoko can have a future, imaging one where it becomes celebrated worldwide for its art scene and attractions, like Venice. Although the artist has never visited Venice, his works blend lived experiences with imaginative possibilities. Using a palette of blues and browns, these compositions feature a unique, cloudy bird’s-eye perspective that makes viewers feel as though they are surveying the landscape from above or sharing the artist’s vision of what lies on the other side. By intertwining Makoko’s floating structures with iconic Venetian landmarks like Santa Maria della Salute, Opedun uses light and architectural elements to blur geographic boundaries and reflect on how history, wealth, and culture shape how communities are valued.

Buqaqawuli Nobakada at Affinity Gallery Image Credit: Emi Eleode for ARTnews Cape Town–based artist Buqaqawuli Nobakada uses her mixed-media practice to look into “mass manifesting” abundance and leisure for Black women. Emcimbini (2026), for example, is a lace-on-canvas painting depicting a vibrant poolside scene with several women lounging on beach chairs and swimming. Having grown up witnessing the socio-economic restrictions and struggles faced by previous generations of women, Nobakada uses her art to project them into aspirational realities. Her canvases become a generational meeting place, allowing women to comfortably inhabit spaces of pleasure and freedom without needing permission. Rather than viewing manifestation as an individual pursuit, the artist frames it as a collective expansion of what is possible. By incorporating delicate lace, Nobakada adds a layer to these ordinary yet historically restricted moments of belonging, extending possibilities into the past and ensuring the women who shaped her experiences are included in these newly imagined futures of joy.

Medhat Shafik at Errm Art Gallery Image Credit: Emi Eleode for ARTnews Unveiling a new collection of texturally rich paintings, Egyptian artist Medhat Shafik applies art as a metaphor for the fractures in contemporary society. Working like an archaeologist, he merges pieces together in what he calls “fragments” to help society reconnect with a sense of collective identity amid global conflict. The booth’s centerpiece, a layered collage painting titled Red (2025), introduces the otherworldly into this discussion, as seen via an asteroid hurtling toward Earth in this red-dominated composition. His practice is rooted in mystery and draws inspiration from ancient Mediterranean, Middle Eastern, and Nile heritages. He builds his canvases from a variety of materials, including natural sand, teabags, and fabrics treated with Indian dyeing techniques. This focus on materiality gives the artwork an organic quality, inviting viewers to look beyond the surface and discover the hidden meanings behind the abstract shapes, revealing a shared human narrative.

Yvanovitch Mbaya at Ablakassa Image Credit: Emi Eleode for ARTnews Exploring themes of belonging, memory and cultural identity, Congolese artist Yvanovitch Mbaya’s massive textile showpiece, Untitled (2023), takes center stage in the room. Crafted from recycled denim, a fabric also used to cover trucks transporting commercial goods, Mbaya repurposes this rugged material as an homage to his people. On its surface, anonymous, genderless figures from the Bantu tribe appear. Using coffee and oil paint, he infuses the heavy denim with materials that create varied textures and an earthy presence. Also on view are two works on paper, demonstrating the artist’s multidisciplinary transition between canvas and paper. He also takes inspiration from his academic background in art psychology and his physical journeys across Africa. Mbaya’s installation balances individual memory, capturing how people and their material histories continuously shape one another.

Mellaney Roberts at Berman Contemporary Gallery Image Credit: Emi Eleode for ARTnews Mellaney Roberts, a ceramic artist and academic from South Africa, transforms clay, glass, and metal into vessels of remembrance. Originally from Willowmore in the Eastern Cape, Roberts has created three sculptures for the fair, exploring themes of identity, material memory, and land-based narratives. Her latest body of work emerges from a place of mourning following the devastating floods in May 2026, which washed away ancestral lands belonging to marginalized Coloured and Khoi communities in South Africa. To honor this history and repair fractured legacies, Roberts focuses on materiality, sourcing clay, resin, and tree bark collected from her home region. Her standing sculpture, Die Draers (The Bearers), 2026, has a touch of the steampunk aesthetic, integrating copper into the cut and pierced ceramic surfaces. The works function as metaphors for shifting cultural borders and classifications. Roberts’s hybrid forms conjure intergenerational memories, subverting discourses of otherness and challenging the painful feeling of non-belonging.

Alpha Odhiambo at 16/16 Image Credit: Emi Eleode for ARTnews Self-taught, Nairobi-based artist Alpha Odhiambo presents a technical showcase of a unique painting method he’s spent years perfecting. He works exclusively on industrial vinyl mesh, as seen in his multilayered piece Bodybuilder (2026). Odhiambo meticulously mixes acrylics and solvent paints to achieve a precise viscosity that prevents pigment from seeping through the porous screen. The resulting work balances opacity and translucency, resembling stained-glass windows or shifting holograms. The piece also changes under different lighting conditions, adding to its dynamic nature. Odhiambo is inspired by the imagery from daily life to analyze global political structures and their impact on human livelihoods, with his layered mesh works serving as a mirror to power. He invites viewers to interpret his work and shows how technical precision can become a catalyst for critical societal engagement.

Souad Abdelrasoul at Gallery Misr Image Credit: Emi Eleode for ARTnews Artist and art historian Souad Abdelrasoul, who lives and works in Cairo, employs surreal, metamorphosed figures to explore the tension between progressive women and oppressive social and cultural systems. Her large-scale centerpiece painting, A Memory Between Fear and Flowers (2026), depicts a silent psychological confrontation between a contemporary woman and a man in primitive clothing, shaped by the past. He holds a rabbit, symbolizing unanalyzed fears and the masculine authority that society imposes, in which male vulnerability has no room to be expressed, while the woman clutches a miniature mirror image of herself. This reflection serves as an archive of maternal lineage, representing a future loved one, such as her daughter, and generations of inherited resilience. In addition to the main canvas, her exhibition includes six smaller dual-aspect portraits of faces. Together, these works examine how love, silence, and trauma are passed down through generations, creating a visual narrative that encourages women to liberate themselves from fears that weren’t theirs to begin with.

Kimathi Mafafo at Kristin Hjellegjerde Image Credit: Courtesy the artist and Kristin Hjellegjerde In a vibrant solo exhibition featuring seven intricate embroidered textile works, South African artist Kimathi Mafafo surveys nature as an embodied experience of female empowerment. Created with both hand and machine stitching, her works employ varied stitches that resemble rich brushstrokes, blending layers of pink, purple, and brown to achieve skin tones. Collaboration is central to Mafafo’s practice: She works closely with women she has trained in her studio, weaving elements of their lives into layered surfaces. This spirit of collective solidarity appears in Clearly, A Flamboyant Alliance: A Flamboyant Collaboration (2023), where overlapping limbs create a hybrid quality, as if the bodies are in motion. Drawing on childhood memories of visiting botanical gardens, Mafafo incorporates lush passion flowers into her tapestries. Her grandmother introduced her to this calming flower for its restorative properties, and it becomes a mystical transmitter of serenity. Mafafo’s sculptural fabrics offer a meditative quality, inviting introspection and nurturing energy that extends well beyond the canvas edges.

title_original: Storia del manto blu della Vergine, un’icona tra tradizione e libertà pittorica
editorial_title_zh: 圣母蓝色斗篷的故事：介于传统与绘画自由之间的图像
editorial_excerpt_zh: 圣母斗篷的颜色，从珍贵的青金石到文艺复兴时期的种种变体：一部漫长而丰富的象征、艺术交流与绘画自由的历史。文章《圣母蓝色斗篷的故事：介于传统与绘画自由之间的图像》源自……

"圣母的蓝色斗篷是西方圣母图像中最为人熟悉的标志之一。在中世纪晚期与文艺复兴之间，与天堂尊严和玛丽亚纯洁相联系的蓝色，也兼具了声望的价值。其中最受追捧的是天然群青，它提取自主要产自今阿富汗巴达赫尚地区的青金石。这种青金石极为罕见且价值连城，其价值堪比黄金甚至超过黄金。因此，将其运用在玛丽亚的斗篷上，也增添了图像的珍贵感。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.exibart.com/repository/media/2026/10/Virgin_of_Vladimir.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "弗拉基米尔的圣母（Theotokos di Vladimir），12世纪，104×69 cm，莫斯科特列季亚科夫画廊", "credit": "Exibart", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "来自保加利亚内塞巴尔的慈悲圣母（La Vergine Eleousa），13-14世纪，板面蛋彩画", "credit": "Exibart", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在文艺复兴时期，圣母子画像深深扎根于拜占庭传统——在拜占庭传统中，圣母的斗篷尚未系统性地呈现蓝色——随后在西方被重新拾起并加以诠释。在各种范式中，被称为Ἐλεούσα（Eleousa）的温柔圣母以母子之间极度的亲密感而著称。他们的面庞相触，常常面颊贴着面颊，而圣母子则紧紧相依或互相拥抱。温柔之中又融入了一种更加严肃的维度，这与对受难（Passione）的预示息息相关。在15世纪，多纳泰罗及其周边圈子在意大利重启了这一图式，赋予其更强烈的人性和心理张力。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.exibart.com/repository/media/2026/10/Foto-2-Madonna.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "罗希尔·范德韦登（Rogier Van der Weyden），《杜兰圣母》（Madonna Durán），1435-1438，西班牙马德里普拉多博物馆；罗希尔·范德韦登圈子，《持康乃馨的圣母》（Vergine con il garofano），约1480，根特美术博物馆（Museum voor Schone Kunsten）", "credit": "Exibart", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "低地国家（古代尼德兰）绘画的影响正是建立这一传统基础之上。扬·凡·艾克、罗希尔·范德韦登及其同代人的作品在意大利广泛流传，其间的油画、罩染、光线与皮肤质感令艺术家们着迷。安东内罗·达·墨西拿在这些交流中占据了至关重要的角色。他可能曾在那不勒斯师从科拉兰托尼奥（Colantonio），深受佛兰芒绘画以及扬·凡·艾克范式的影响。阿拉贡的阿方索（Alfonso d'Aragona）宫廷当时是接受北方绘画的重要中心。安东内罗吸收了其中的创新，经常使用深色背景，将光线聚焦于面庞，从而增强其存在感。圣母衣物的颜色也可能偏离传统蓝色，呈现出更温暖的色调。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这种绘画方式在米兰也得到了呼应。早在1460年，比安卡·玛丽亚·维斯孔蒂·斯福尔扎就派遣米兰画家扎内托·布加托（Zanetto Bugatto）前往布鲁塞尔，以便师从罗希尔·范德韦登。布加托于1463年返回米兰。因此，当达芬奇大约二十年后抵达该城市时，与北方绘画的对话已经相当巩固。这种敏感性后来在其圈子的艺术家中得以延续，尤其是马克·多焦诺（Marco d’Oggiono）和贝纳尔迪诺·卢伊尼（Bernardino Luini），他们描绘的一些圣母斗篷呈现出红色、赭色或大地色调，并且常常置于深色背景之上。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.exibart.com/repository/media/2026/10/Foto-4-Madonna.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "贝纳尔迪诺·卢伊尼，《圣母子》，约1515-1520，那不勒斯卡波迪蒙特博物馆和皇家树林；马克·多焦诺（传），《圣母子》，约1516；马克·多焦诺，《圣母子》，约1520", "credit": "Exibart", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "然而，面对我们今天所看到的颜色，必须保持谨慎。一些今天看起来呈深色的斗篷最初其实是蓝色的。随着时间的推移，由于颜料和画层的老化，它们的外观已经发生了改变。如今，科学分析使我们能够将这些转变与画家最初选择的颜色区分开来。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "然而，乔瓦尼·贝利尼的案例表明，红色也可能对应着一种真正的绘画选择。在他作坊的一幅作于1475年前后并经英国国家美术馆分析的圣母子画像中，玛丽亚穿着一件红色的斗篷。贝利尼本人也在多幅构图中使用了这种颜色。英国国家美术馆强调了这一选择的不寻常之处，不过这也与当时的艺术背景息息相关。事实上，这件作品的创作时间恰逢安东内罗·达·墨西拿驻留威尼斯期间。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.exibart.com/repository/media/2026/10/Foto-5-Madonna.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "乔瓦尼·贝利尼（作坊），《圣母子》或《瞻礼沉睡圣童的圣母》（Madonna in adorazione del Bambino dormiente），约1475；乔瓦尼·贝利尼（传），《圣母子》，约1470，罗维戈协和学院美术馆（Pinacoteca dell’Accademia dei Concordi）；乔瓦尼·贝利尼，《维特根斯坦圣母》（Madonna Wittgenstein），约1485", "credit": "Exibart", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "因此，蓝色斗篷的历史表明，一幅熟悉的图像如何可能演变成一种虚假的确定性。在我们的想象中与玛丽亚深度绑定的蓝色，从未构成过一成不变的规则。在文艺复兴时期，范式、技术和色彩不断流转与蜕变。艺术永不凝固。", "translated": true}]

article_text:
Il manto blu della Vergine è uno dei segni più familiari dell’iconografia mariana occidentale. Tra la fine del Medioevo e il Rinascimento, il blu, associato alla dignità celeste e alla purezza di Maria, assume anche un valore di prestigio. Il più ricercato era l’oltremare naturale, ricavato dal lapislazzuli proveniente soprattutto dal Badakhshan, nell’attuale Afghanistan. Raro e costosissimo, poteva valere quanto l’oro o persino più dell’oro. Il suo impiego nel manto di Maria contribuiva così alla preziosità dell’immagine.

Nel Rinascimento, le rappresentazioni della Vergine col Bambino affondano le radici nella tradizione bizantina – dove il manto della Vergine non è ancora sistematicamente blu -, poi ripresa e reinterpretata in Occidente. Tra i diversi modelli, la Vergine della tenerezza, detta Ἐλεούσα, Eleousa, si distingue per l’estrema vicinanza tra Madre e Bambino. I loro volti si toccano, spesso guancia a guancia, mentre il Bambino si stringe alla madre o la abbraccia. Alla tenerezza si unisce una dimensione più grave, legata alla prefigurazione della Passione. Nel XV secolo, Donatello e il suo ambiente riprendono questa formula in Italia, conferendole maggiore intensità umana e psicologica.

Su questa tradizione si innesta l’influenza della pittura degli antichi Paesi Bassi. Le opere di Jan van Eyck, Rogier van der Weyden e dei loro contemporanei circolano in Italia, dove la pittura a olio, le velature, la luce e gli incarnati affascinano gli artisti. Antonello da Messina occupa un ruolo essenziale in questi scambi. Probabilmente formatosi a Napoli presso Colantonio , è profondamente segnato dalla pittura fiamminga e dai modelli di Jan van Eyck. La corte di Alfonso d’Aragona è allora un importante centro di ricezione della pittura nordica. Antonello ne assimila le innovazioni, utilizzando spesso fondi scuri che concentrano la luce sui volti e ne intensificano la presenza. Anche i colori degli abiti della Vergine possono allontanarsi dal blu tradizionale e assumere tonalità più calde.

Questo modo di dipingere trova un’eco anche a Milano. Già nel 1460, Bianca Maria Visconti Sforza invia il pittore milanese Zanetto Bugatto a Bruxelles affinché si formi presso Rogier van der Weyden. Bugatto rientra a Milano nel 1463. Quando Leonardo da Vinci arriva in città circa vent’anni più tardi, il dialogo con la pittura nordica è quindi già ben consolidato. Questa sensibilità si ritrova in seguito negli artisti della sua cerchia, in particolare Marco d’Oggiono e Bernardino Luini , che raffigurano alcuni manti della Vergine assumono tonalità rosse, ocra o terrose, spesso su fondi scuri.

Occorre tuttavia essere prudenti di fronte ai colori che vediamo oggi. Alcuni manti oggi scuri erano originariamente blu. Il loro aspetto si è modificato nel tempo, a causa dell’invecchiamento dei pigmenti e degli strati pittorici. Le analisi scientifiche permettono oggi di distinguere queste trasformazioni dal colore scelto originariamente dal pittore.

Il caso di Giovanni Bellini mostra tuttavia che il rosso poteva anche corrispondere a una vera scelta pittorica. In una Vergine col Bambino della sua bottega, datata intorno al 1475 e analizzata dalla National Gallery, Maria indossa un manto rosso. Bellini stesso utilizza questo colore in diverse composizioni. La National Gallery sottolinea il carattere insolito di questa scelta, che può tuttavia essere messa in relazione con il contesto artistico dell’epoca. La data di realizzazione di quest’opera coincide infatti con il soggiorno veneziano di Antonello da Messina.

Così, la storia del manto blu mostra come un’immagine familiare possa diventare una falsa certezza. Il blu, profondamente associato a Maria nel nostro immaginario, non ha mai costituito una regola immutabile. Nel Rinascimento, i modelli, le tecniche e i colori circolano e si trasformano. L’arte non è mai immobile.

article_text:
We still have to wait until May 2027 for Curry Barker ‘s “Anything But Ghosts” to hit theaters , but fans of the “Obsession” writer/director have a new project to tide them over.

Barker has written, directed, and edited a new short film titled “ Mama Bear ,” which was released on his That’s a Bad Idea YouTube channel on Thursday morning. The five-minute project, which was sponsored by Microsoft, stars Jon Lee Richardson as Floyd, a young man whose nap is interrupted by some very disturbing phone calls that quickly change the course of his day. Katie Sarife, Ericka Kreuz, and Joshua Snyder co-star. Check out the film below.

Barker continues to enjoy one of the biggest breakout years we’ve seen from a filmmaker in recent memory. After “Obsession” was acquired by Focus Features at the 2025 Toronto International Film Festival, it went on to gross over $500 million at the global box office this spring. Barker quickly became one of Hollywood’s most in-demand filmmakers, lining up a slate of projects that includes a “Texas Chainsaw Massacre” reboot for A24 and a mysterious original horror movie that landed him an eight-figure deal from Universal. And Barker had already completed “Anything But Ghosts,” a supernatural comedy that sees him co-star with his longtime filmmaking partner Cooper Tomlinson, before “Obsession” even opened.

It led to Barker receiving IndieWire’s inaugural Future of Filmmaking Award at our recent Los Angeles summit. During a conversation with IndieWire’s Chris O’Falt at the event, Barker spoke about his roots making independent short films and how it helped him refine his voice ahead of “Obsession.”

“I definitely learned from the comment section quite a bit,” Barker said of his experiencing posting his shorts on the That’s a Bad Idea channel. “I think the main thing I would take away is how smart the audience is. I think if I hadn’t learned that early on, I might write my dialogue differently. Maybe I’d write more exposition, maybe I’d not feel so confident that people were understanding me. That was invaluable, to see ‘Oh my god, this little thing, they are picking up on it! They are understanding these nuances.’”
excerpt_original: The five-minute film, which Barker wrote, directed, and edited, was released on his That's a Bad Idea YouTube channel.

Thing”。她曾任费城当代艺术研究所副策展人、洛杉矶地下博物馆联合总监兼策展人，并于2023年以特聘策展人身份加入惠特尼美术馆。次年，她晋升为以捐赠者命名的南希与弗雷德·波泽兹策展人。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "paragraph", "text": "另一方面，涉足歌剧和戏剧等领域的维诺库尔是美国现代歌剧公司（American Modern Opera Company，AMOC*）的共同创始人。该团体于2025年在林肯中心举办了为期5周的艺术节，推出了12部新作。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "维诺库尔导演的作品包括在费城歌剧院上演的《Complications in Sue》《The Black Clown》等。他还制作了为纪念A24与迪奥合作、由贾斯汀·维维安·邦德（Justin Vivian Bond）主演的《Both Ends》。在库珀-休伊特史密森尼设计三年展中，他与休·海登（Hugh Hayden）、达沃内·泰恩斯（Davóne Guerrero）和德鲁·索耶（Drew Sawyer）担任策展人的这一届吸引了超过55万名观众，并于10月12日闭幕。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "谈及与昂利的合作，维诺库尔在声明中这样说道：", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“我们双方都希望将焦点放在物与人、以及二者碰撞交汇之处。这种想法已经在我们的合作中显现出来。正因为拥有这种能量，与她的对话才如此愉快且充满启发。作为一名艺术家，最令我心潮澎湃的莫过于为其他艺术家竭尽全力。我很高兴能在惠特尼这个舞台上获得这样的机会。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "惠特尼美术馆馆长斯科特·罗斯科夫谈到了双年展期间产生的“策展的独特色学反应”，并对两人寄予了以下厚望：", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“梅格是当今策展界中最迷人的面孔之一。她拥有非凡的力量，能够支持艺术家并为美国艺术史带来新的视角。扎克同样是一位具有创造艺术项目天赋的人才。通过跨越歌剧、戏剧、舞蹈和视觉艺术的开创性工作，他已成为同代人中最具代表性的人物之一。两人的合作将为2028年的双年展带来革新性的愿景。”（翻译：编辑部）", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", article_text:
2028年ホイットニー・ビエンナーレのキュレーターが決定。舞台芸術とアートの新たな接点へ

2028年3月に開幕する第83回 ホイットニー・ビエンナーレ の共同キュレーターが決定した。同館のメグ・オンリとともに、オペラや演劇を手がけるザック・ウィノカーが起用され、舞台芸術とアートの新たな接点に期待が寄せられる。

ホイットニー美術館 が2年に1度開催する、 アメリカ を代表する芸術祭「 ホイットニー・ビエンナーレ 」。絵画や彫刻から映像、インスタレーション、パフォーマンスまで幅広い表現を紹介する同展は、2028年3月に次回の開幕を迎える。このほど、その共同キュレーターに、同館のメグ・オンリ（Meg Onli）と演出家のザック・ウィノカー（Zack Winokur）が任命された。

オンリが同ビエンナーレを手がけるのは、今回で2度目だ。2024年には、クリッシー・アイルズ（Chrissie Iles）とともに「Even Better Than the Real Thing」を企画した。彼女はフィラデルフィアの現代美術研究所でアソシエイト・キュレーター、ロサンゼルスのアンダーグラウンド・ミュージアムで共同ディレクター兼キュレーターを歴任し、2023年に特任キュレーターとしてホイットニー美術館に加わった。翌年には、寄付者の名を冠したナンシー＆フレッド・ポーゼズ・キュレーターに昇格している。

また、アーティストの アレックス・ダ・コルテ とともに、同館で2026年10月に開幕した ロイ・リキテンスタイン の回顧展も共同企画している。US版ARTnews副編集長のアレックス・グリーンバーガーは、これを「洗練された展覧会」と 評価した 。ポップアートの巨匠リキテンスタインが、「イメージに取りつかれた現代の到来を予見していた……さらには、その流れを意図的に後押ししてさえいた」という見方を提示する展覧会だと評している。

アーティストであるダ・コルテとの共同企画は、次回のビエンナーレでオンリとウィノカーの協働がどのように展開するかを考える手がかりになるかもしれない。美術館はプレスリリースで、2人は「今日の芸術実践を幅広く捉える視点を持ち、アーティストを支え、実験を促し、分野を横断する新たな可能性を探ろうとする姿勢を共有している」と説明した。

オンリは声明で、次のように意気込みを語った。

「ホイットニー・ビエンナーレに再び携われることを、とてもうれしく思います。初期の年次展『アニュアル』から、その後のさまざまな展開に至るまで、この展覧会は幾度も姿を変えてきました。その豊かな歴史は、すでに私たちに多くの考える材料を与えてくれています。発想豊かなザックとともにビエンナーレの可能性を探り、アーティストたちとの対話がどこへ導いてくれるのかを見届けることが、楽しみでなりません」

一方、オペラや演劇などを手がけるウィノカーは、アメリカン・モダン・オペラ・カンパニー（American Modern Opera Company、AMOC*）の共同創設者だ。同団体は2025年、リンカーン・センターで5週間にわたるフェスティバルを開催し、12の新作を発表した。

ウィノカーの演出作には、オペラ・フィラデルフィアで上演された《Complications in Sue》《The Black Clown》などがある。また、A24とディオールの提携を記念し、ジャスティン・ヴィヴィアン・ボンド（Justin Vivian Bond）が主演した《Both Ends》も手がけた。クーパー・ヒューイット・スミソニアン・デザイン・トリエンナーレでは、ヒュー・ヘイデン（Hugh Hayden）、ダヴォーン・タインズ（Davóne Tines）とインスタレーションを共同制作するなど、視覚芸術の分野でも活動している。だが、これまで大規模な美術館展のキュレーションを手がけたことのないウィノカーの起用は異例とも言えるとアートネットは 報じている 。

また、ニューヨークの水上公園リトル・アイランドの元芸術監督でもある。同施設は2026年のホイットニー・ビエンナーレの会場の1つとなり、8月にはフリオ・トーレス（Julio Torres）とマーティーヌ・グティエレス（Martine Gutierrez）によるパフォーマンス《Marina》が上演された。マルセラ・ゲレロ（Marcela Guerrero）とドリュー・ソーヤー（Drew Sawyer）がキュレーターを務めたこの回は、55万人以上の来場者を集め、10月12日に閉幕した。

オンリとの協働について、ウィノカーは声明でこう述べている。

「私たちはともに、モノと人、そして両者がぶつかり合うところに焦点を当てたいと考えています。その思いは、すでに私たちの協働にも表れています。このエネルギーがあるからこそ、彼女との対話は楽しく、刺激に満ちているのです。アーティストである私にとって、何より心が躍るのは、ほかのアーティストのために力を尽くすことです。ホイットニーという場で、その機会を得られることをうれしく思います」

ホイットニー美術館館長のスコット・ロスコフは、ビエンナーレごとに生まれる「キュレーションの独自の化学反応」に触れながら、2人への期待を次のように語った。

「メグは、今日のキュレーションを担う、最も魅力的な存在の1人です。アーティストを支え、アメリカ美術史に新たな視点をもたらす、並外れた力を持っています。ザックもまた、独創的な芸術プログラムを生み出す才能の持ち主です。オペラ、演劇、ダンス、視覚芸術を横断する画期的な仕事を通じて、同世代を代表する存在の1人となりました。2人の協働は、2028年のビエンナーレに革新的なビジョンをもたらしてくれるでしょう」（翻訳：編集部）

article_text:
Was sind die Tech-Revolutionen der nahen Zukunft? Ein faltbares iPhone sicher nicht. Ein Start-up aus Kalifornien arbeitet an Mützen, die KI-Agenten durch Gehirnströme steuern. Aber wollen wir wirklich auch noch unsere Gedanken verscherbeln?

Wer dieser Tage auf große neue Produkte hofft, dürfte eher enttäuscht werden. Apple hat zwar ein neues MacBook Pro mit Touchscreen vorgestellt, die gibt es von der Konkurrenz aber schon seit vielen Jahren, und eigentlich hatte sich gerade Apple (auch schon unter Steve Jobs) für viele Jahre mit Händen und Füßen dagegen gewehrt, weil es das Konzept als weder ergonomisch noch alltagstauglich abtat.

Das iPhone Duo mit Faltdisplay versprach ebenso, alles besser zu machen als die Konkurrenz von Samsung und Co., aber auch hier kam es wenige Tage nach Auslieferung zu kaputten Displays und verbogenen Gehäusen. Nun hat Apple also nach " Antennagate " (das Anfassen des iPhone 4 an einer bestimmten Stelle verursachte Probleme) und "Bendgate" (das iPhone 6 ließ sich verbiegen) einen weiteren Skandal an der Backe: "Crackgate". Der Start des neuen CEO John Ternus hätte besser laufen können. Fairerweise muss man aber sagen, dass die Produkte natürlich schon vor seinem Amtseintritt als Apple-Boss entwickelt und geplant wurden.

Wo geht es also hin mit der Technik, die unsere Welt verbessern soll? Ein Start-up aus dem kalifornischen Palo Alto mit dem Namen Sabi hat da eine Idee. Schon heute nutzen viele Menschen statt einer Tastatur die Sprachsteuerung, um ChatGPT, ihr Smart Home oder das Infotainment des Autos zu steuern. Einigen, mich eingeschlossen, ist das Quatschen mit Maschinen allerdings immer noch suspekt.

Mütze statt Gehirnchip

Das liegt zum einen daran, dass es oft zu Missverständnissen zwischen Mensch und Maschine kommt und dementsprechend zu nicht zufriedenstellenden Ergebnissen. Bei mir ist das Plaudern mit Smartphone oder Computer aber auch zu schambehaftet. Ein bisschen so, wie ich mich Ende der 90er mit meinem Nokia 5210 auch heimlich in eine Ecke verkrochen habe, um damit zu telefonieren. Diese Scham kenne ich heute natürlich kaum noch.

Sabi entwickelt Mützen. Eine Wollmütze und eine Baseballkappe befinden sich in der Planung. Es handelt sich um Wearables, die mithilfe von Elektroenzephalographie (EEG) Gehirnaktivitäten analysieren und zur Steuerung von Computern nutzen wollen. An solchen Konzepten, sogenannten Brain-Computer-Interfaces (BCI), arbeiten Firmen wie Elon Musks Neuralink schon eine ganze Weile. Nur mit dem Unterschied, dass Neuralink chirurgisch implantiert werden muss.

Sabi soll unterdessen ganz ohne Eingriff funktionieren. Hier sind die Kopfbedeckungen mit zahlreichen Sensoren ausgestattet. Statt "Speech-to-Text" ist es jetzt also "Think-to-Text", was Investoren und Gründer gerade hypen. Mit BCI können heute schon Videogames gespielt und sogar Musik gemacht werden.

Wenn das Gehirn die KI-Agenten steuert

Für Sabis CEO Rahul Chhabra geht es allerdings weniger darum, mit seinen Mützen WhatsApp-Nachrichten zu schreiben oder nach Kuchenrezepten zu suchen. Das ist nur ein vorläufiger Schritt. Sabi sieht seine Produkte vor allem in der Steuerung von KI-Agenten. Gedanken werden gelesen, analysiert und dann in passende Prompts übersetzt.

Wozu KI-Agenten heute schon in der Lage sind, liest man in diesen Wochen immer wieder in den Nachrichten. Während ein Großteil heute KI als Suchmaschinen-Ersatz nutzt, hacken Profis mit KI-Agenten Regierungsseiten oder legen ganze Netzwerke lahm .

Gerade im Kontext der weltweiten Cybersecurity sehen viele IT-Experten ziemlich düstere Zeiten auf uns zukommen. Auch der aktuell gemeldete, mutmaßlich nordkoreanische Hack der Kryptobörse Binance dürfte mit Hilfe von KI-Agenten umgesetzt worden sein.

Die Gedanken sind nicht mehr frei

Die Mützen von Sabi sollen auf der kommenden CES, einem wichtigen Tech-Event in Las Vegas Anfang 2027, als Prototyp vorgestellt werden. Zwar ist noch nicht bekannt, wie teuer so ein Interface werden wird und wie praktikabel es überhaupt ist. Fest steht aber, wohin es mit dem Computing in den kommenden Jahren gehen wird. Die QWERTZ-Tastatur ist letztlich auch ein Relikt aus längst vergangenen Schreibmaschinenzeiten, wurde sie doch schon 1868 von Christopher Latham Sholes patentiert.

Auch jüngere Menschen arbeiten heute kaum noch mit Tastaturen und können nicht ordentlich blind tippen. Wieso dann nicht gleich die intimsten Wünsche, Träume und Ideen von einem kommerziellen Tech-Start-up aus dem Silicon Valley speichern und analysieren lassen, um damit Maschinen zu steuern?

Die größenwahnsinnige Vision, so etwas wie die Marvel-Figur Professor X zu sein (m ö gen Sie in Frieden ruhen, Sir Patrick Stewart), die mit Telepathie zu Mächtigem fähig ist, überlagert hier einen menschlichen Freiheitskampf, der viele Jahrhunderte dauerte und unzählige Opfer forderte. Die Gedanken sind dann nicht mehr frei - und jeder kann sie erraten.

article_text:
EXCLUSIVE: Storied British producer Pippa Harris and YouTube UK boss Alison Lomax have joined the board of Britain’s National Film and Television School ( NFTS ).

The pair join the likes of BBC content boss Kate Phillips and Sky Studios CEO Cécile Frot-Coutaz on the governors board.

They bring together film and TV production expertise with digital as the school continues to evolve, according to the NFTS.

Double Oscar nominee Harris is the founder of Neal Street and has been behind the likes of 1917, Call the Midwife and Hamnet. Upcoming she has Sam Mendes’ quartet of Beatles movies. As YouTube UK and Ireland boss for nearly four years, Lomax occupies a different lane. She has overseen serious growth for the Google-owned platform in the UK and has impressed traditional TV executives along the way.

Related Stories

YouTube Ad Revenue Rises 9% But Parent Alphabet Misses Wall Street's Q3 Targets; Stock Drops

Entertainment Hits $332.5B To Become World's Second Most Valuable Sector As Netflix, YouTube & Spotify Fly - Interbrand Report

Alongside Harris, Lomax, Phillips and Frot-Coutaz, the NFTS board is comprised of Roughcut TV founder Ash Atalla , Film4 Director Farhana Bhula, ITV Studios MD Julian Bellamy and ex-Warner Bros. Discovery VP Polly Cochrane.

Watch on Deadline

The appointments come at a significant moment for the NFTS as it prepares to open The Cubby Broccoli Building at its Beaconsfield HQ in January 2027. Supported by government and industry investment, the school’s expansion will provide 25,000 sq. ft. of additional teaching space, house new courses, expand apprenticeship opportunities and provide accessible student accommodation for the first time in its history.

NFTS Chair Sophie Turner Laing said: “The way audiences discover, engage with and enjoy stories is changing at an extraordinary pace, and it’s vital the NFTS continues to reflect the full breadth of the industries our graduates are being trained to enter. Pippa and Alison bring hugely valuable and complementary perspectives, from the craft and ambition behind some of the world’s most successful film and television productions to the phenomenal growth of digital creators and new platforms. Both are exceptional leaders with a real commitment to creative talent, and I’m delighted they will be bringing their insight and experience to the Board at such an important moment for the School.”

Harris added: “It is an honour to be joining the Board of Governors at the NFTS. The strength of our industry ultimately depends on the talent coming through and on ensuring that people from all backgrounds have the opportunity to develop their skills, find their voice and build lasting careers. The NFTS has an extraordinary track record of nurturing creative talent and I’m very much looking forward to playing a part in its next chapter.”

Lomax said: “The National Film and Television School is globally renowned as a world-class training ground for craft, technical excellence, and storytelling. Its educational mission has never been more relevant as traditional production and creator-led entertainment increasingly converge. Through YouTube’s NFTS partnerships, including our Creator Incubator and Create x Connect, I’ve been deeply impressed with the School and am committed to opening access, building digital skills nationwide and championing the next generation of creative talent.”

article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "The latest edition, A Chorus of Strangers , feels much like the reality of Britain today – confused, messed up, angry, threatening and full of mixed messages"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Between the skeleton of Dippy the Diplodocus (which has ‘stomped’ – according to promotional materials – all the way from the Natural History Museum in London to be with us at Coventry’s Herbert Art Gallery & Museum) and an exhibition about marine life in the county of Warwickshire when it was submerged during the Jurassic Period, you’ll find one of three parts of the quinquennial British Art Show (BAS). And unlike those souvenirs of yesterday, the BAS – this tenth edition curated by writer, curator, broadcaster and former Institute of Contemporary Arts director Ekow Eshun – promises to bring us bang up to date: on the state of art (the works on show, by 37 artists, have been made over the past five years) and of the nation (this is roughly the period since Britain officially left the European Union) today. By the time you get to the cutting-edge contemporary you’ll be inescapably aware that the venue itself is set up (like so many British cultural institutions) to distract us from our inglorious present with displays of a supposedly glorious past."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Even so, cutting-edge contemporary might not be the first thing that comes to mind when you encounter the first work in the BAS display: Lindsey Mendick’s series of clay sculptures, Wicked Game (2025), arranged as if part of a fragmented, almost lifesize chess set, featuring anthropomorphised animal pieces (exuding the faint whiff of Beatrix Potter characters) that look like the fractured remains (held together by pins and armatures) of an antique sculpture garden. In fact, you’ll likely feel that it only adds a further dreamlike varnish to the all-our-yesterdays vibe that permeates this institution. A wall text tells us that Mendick’s work combines the history of Queen Elizabeth I (here she’s a lion) and female characters from Ancient Greek mythology to evoke the story of the queen’s celebrated refusal to marry. It’s unclear if this is about viewing the past through a feminist lens, or if it’s suggesting that feminism is nothing new. Or perhaps a sense of animism or closeness to nature is more the point. Installed on the museum’s ground floor, just around the corner from Dippy, it blends in so seamlessly with the rest of the Herbert’s displays that it’s hard to imagine what more it might be telling us. Upstairs, however, where the bulk of the BAS display is housed, it’s literally another story."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Installation-view-of-Lindsey-Mendick-Wicked-Game-2025-in-British-Art-Show-10_-A-Chorus-of-Strangers.-Image-courtesy-the-artist-and-Hayward-Gallery-Touring.-Photo_-David-Parry.-1230x820.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "Lindsey Mendick, Wicked Game , 2025, installation view in A Chorus of Strangers. Unlike Alex Margo Arden’s Accounts (2025), a giant bouquet of 11 lifesize white male mannequins representing various trades of mid-twentieth-century Britain – milkmen, butchers, bus conductors, labourers. It brings to mind the extras from a BBC production of a Miss Marple detective story. Somewhat ghoulish and somewhat broken (the odd missing hand or foot), they’re each frozen in the middle of some sort of action or reaction and collectively roped together into a sad, confused, but sometimes angry-looking mass. And perhaps they’ve got something to be upset about: castoffs from scrapped dioramas at the National Motor Museum in Hampshire, they’ve gone the way of the dinosaurs. A bit like the British automobile industry itself (vehicle production today is at its lowest since 1952). But while all that (the Motor Museum info is on a wall label) might tempt you to interpret the work as a wry nod to Coventry’s status as the birthplace of the dying British automobile industry, Hussain and Gunaratne’s work, Here Is The Brick (2025), gives it a rather different, more sinister spin."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The title of the work derives from the story of a brick thrown in the face of an Asian shopkeeper (he’s shown in news footage, clutching the offensive object, which smashed his teeth, near the beginning of the video). The remainder of the work is a fast-paced mashup of found footage documenting other instances of violence, outright racism and its opposite: the fawning acceptance of British South Asian and Muslim individuals when they do something of which the nation can be proud. Generally in the field of sports, where race doesn’t matter, apparently, when you’re winning (we see athlete Mo Farah, or boxer Naseem Hamed). It’s all epitomised in the chants of adulation we hear for former Liverpool football star Mohamed Salah: “If he’s good enough for you, he’s good enough for me, if he scores another few, then I’ll be Muslim too / If he’s good enough for you, he’s good enough for me, he’s sitting in a mosque, that’s where I want to be.” Before being quickly undone by a series of references to ‘Fucking Pakis’. Beside the monitor is a wall filled by Hussain’s Mosque City: Birmingham’s Spiritual Landscape (2023–25), casual photographs of 160 mosques: some that look like mosques (with minarets); others that don’t, these last blending almost seamlessly into domestic settings, warehouses or Birmingham’s commercial high streets. After you’ve seen the video, you’re aware of the extent to which some people might view this as a portrait of assimilation, while others might see it as infiltration. Now you look back at Arden’s white mannequins (which are in the same gallery) thinking they may have been restrained for the protection of nonwhite visitors. It’s a clever piece of curating that in many ways captures something of the reality of Britain today – confused, messed up, angry, threatening and full of mixed messages. Sometimes, as any good therapist will tell you, it’s better just to let it all out."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Over at the Mead Gallery, it’s the sense of the contingency of ‘Britishness’ that comes to the fore. Looking like a giant’s drying rack, it captures all the messiness, ephemerality and fragility of the past in a way that the general exhibits at the Herbert seemingly seek to ignore. And of course the run of works here seeks to emphasise that British art, and artists working in Britain, derives from many influences that might not be located on a clump of relatively tiny islands floating off the edge of mainland Europe and may not also take one particular shape or form. The suggestion being, of course, that ideas of ‘Britishness’ could work in a similar way. article_text:
The latest edition, A Chorus of Strangers , feels much like the reality of Britain today – confused, messed up, angry, threatening and full of mixed messages

Between the skeleton of Dippy the Diplodocus (which has ‘stomped’ – according to promotional materials – all the way from the Natural History Museum in London to be with us at Coventry’s Herbert Art Gallery & Museum) and an exhibition about marine life in the county of Warwickshire when it was submerged during the Jurassic Period, you’ll find one of three parts of the quinquennial British Art Show (BAS). And unlike those souvenirs of yesterday, the BAS – this tenth edition curated by writer, curator, broadcaster and former Institute of Contemporary Arts director Ekow Eshun – promises to bring us bang up to date: on the state of art (the works on show, by 37 artists, have been made over the past five years) and of the nation (this is roughly the period since Britain officially left the European Union) today. By the time you get to the cutting-edge contemporary you’ll be inescapably aware that the venue itself is set up (like so many British cultural institutions) to distract us from our inglorious present with displays of a supposedly glorious past.

Even so, cutting-edge contemporary might not be the first thing that comes to mind when you encounter the first work in the BAS display: Lindsey Mendick’s series of clay sculptures, Wicked Game (2025), arranged as if part of a fragmented, almost lifesize chess set, featuring anthropomorphised animal pieces (exuding the faint whiff of Beatrix Potter characters) that look like the fractured remains (held together by pins and armatures) of an antique sculpture garden. In fact, you’ll likely feel that it only adds a further dreamlike varnish to the all-our-yesterdays vibe that permeates this institution. A wall text tells us that Mendick’s work combines the history of Queen Elizabeth I (here she’s a lion) and female characters from Ancient Greek mythology to evoke the story of the queen’s celebrated refusal to marry. It’s unclear if this is about viewing the past through a feminist lens, or if it’s suggesting that feminism is nothing new. Or perhaps a sense of animism or closeness to nature is more the point. Installed on the museum’s ground floor, just around the corner from Dippy, it blends in so seamlessly with the rest of the Herbert’s displays that it’s hard to imagine what more it might be telling us. Upstairs, however, where the bulk of the BAS display is housed, it’s literally another story.

Buried in the middle of it all is a 13-minute video by photographer Mahtab Hussain and filmmaker and writer Guy Gunaratne. Presented on a monitor, with the audio heard through headphones, it’s unobtrusive and unassuming. Unlike Alex Margo Arden’s Accounts (2025), a giant bouquet of 11 lifesize white male mannequins representing various trades of mid-twentieth-century Britain – milkmen, butchers, bus conductors, labourers. It brings to mind the extras from a BBC production of a Miss Marple detective story. Somewhat ghoulish and somewhat broken (the odd missing hand or foot), they’re each frozen in the middle of some sort of action or reaction and collectively roped together into a sad, confused, but sometimes angry-looking mass. And perhaps they’ve got something to be upset about: castoffs from scrapped dioramas at the National Motor Museum in Hampshire, they’ve gone the way of the dinosaurs. A bit like the British automobile industry itself (vehicle production today is at its lowest since 1952). But while all that (the Motor Museum info is on a wall label) might tempt you to interpret the work as a wry nod to Coventry’s status as the birthplace of the dying British automobile industry, Hussain and Gunaratne’s work, Here Is The Brick (2025), gives it a rather different, more sinister spin.

The title of the work derives from the story of a brick thrown in the face of an Asian shopkeeper (he’s shown in news footage, clutching the offensive object, which smashed his teeth, near the beginning of the video). The remainder of the work is a fast-paced mashup of found footage documenting other instances of violence, outright racism and its opposite: the fawning acceptance of British South Asian and Muslim individuals when they do something of which the nation can be proud. Generally in the field of sports, where race doesn’t matter, apparently, when you’re winning (we see athlete Mo Farah, or boxer Naseem Hamed). It’s all epitomised in the chants of adulation we hear for former Liverpool football star Mohamed Salah: “If he’s good enough for you, he’s good enough for me, if he scores another few, then I’ll be Muslim too / If he’s good enough for you, he’s good enough for me, he’s sitting in a mosque, that’s where I want to be.” Before being quickly undone by a series of references to ‘Fucking Pakis’. Beside the monitor is a wall filled by Hussain’s Mosque City: Birmingham’s Spiritual Landscape (2023–25), casual photographs of 160 mosques: some that look like mosques (with minarets); others that don’t, these last blending almost seamlessly into domestic settings, warehouses or Birmingham’s commercial high streets. After you’ve seen the video, you’re aware of the extent to which some people might view this as a portrait of assimilation, while others might see it as infiltration. Now you look back at Arden’s white mannequins (which are in the same gallery) thinking they may have been restrained for the protection of nonwhite visitors. It’s a clever piece of curating that in many ways captures something of the reality of Britain today – confused, messed up, angry, threatening and full of mixed messages. A chorus of strangers who lack any clarity about what being ‘British’ means; or who refuse to accept that any definition of Britishness might be more contingent than necessary.

Lest the medium wasn’t carrying the message, a nearby wall text quotes Jamaican-British cultural-theorist Stuart Hall (who, alongside novelist Virginia Woolf and philosopher Timothy Morton, is one of a trinity of muses for the exhibition): ‘the capacity to live with difference is… the coming question of the twenty-first century’. Next up is Joy Gerrard’s black-and-white paintings of crowds and power, among them Together Alliance March, Protest against the far right (Central London, March 28, 2026) (2026), featuring a crowd formed around a banner featuring the slogan ‘DON’T LET RACIST FARAGE AND REFORM DIVIDE THE COUNTRY’, just in case you’d forgotten that answering Hall’s question remains a work in progress (for non-Brits, Nigel Farage is the leader of the rightwing, anti-immigrant Reform Party). It’s a shame, though, that the polite fury on show here is about as punchy as this British Art Show gets. Sometimes, as any good therapist will tell you, it’s better just to let it all out.

Over at the Mead Gallery, it’s the sense of the contingency of ‘Britishness’ that comes to the fore. In Matthew Krishanu’s dreamlike paintings recalling his mixed-race childhood in the lush landscapes of Bangladesh; or in Nnena Kalu’s rapid and repeated, obsessive even, drawings of spiralling, eyelike vortices; or in Dala Nasser’s Church of St Christopher – Kabr Hiram Qana (2025–26), a reinterpretation of a sixth-century Byzantine basilica from her native Lebanon, now in ruins, reimagined as a wooden frame (recreating the church’s doorway), and hanging fabric cyanotypes standing in for missing mosaics. Looking like a giant’s drying rack, it captures all the messiness, ephemerality and fragility of the past in a way that the general exhibits at the Herbert seemingly seek to ignore. And of course the run of works here seeks to emphasise that British art, and artists working in Britain, derives from many influences that might not be located on a clump of relatively tiny islands floating off the edge of mainland Europe and may not also take one particular shape or form. The suggestion being, of course, that ideas of ‘Britishness’ could work in a similar way. And yet the conventional, sterile, white-cube architecture of the Mead, and the fact that there is a distinct focus on painting and sculpture, means that none of this feels truly unruly: all of it looks like it belongs here, contained in the framework of ‘art’, removed from the domain of ‘life’. Safe. Unreal. Although that might contain some truths in and of itself.

There’s a corrective of sorts over at the Delia Derbyshire Building in Coventry University – which functions as a creative lab (with students going in and out of seminar rooms as BAS viewers seek out the artworks). Here video is the prime medium; Melanie Manchot’s Night Moves (2026) features a series of performers using their bodies to occupy various liminal spaces in nocturnal Bristol via the medium of dance – to a soundtrack that features reggaeton, Yoruba music, jungle and dance forms that range from salsa to classical ballet – in a way that offers an alternative take on the idea of individual and collective agency to that iterated in Gerrard’s paintings of protests and crowded streets. It finds an (real life) echo here in photographs from Liz Johnson Artur’s Black Balloon Archive (2026), featuring dancing bodies (belonging to members of the African diaspora) in clubs, churches and boxing rings; and in Ufuoma Essi’s video Bodies in Dissent (2021), which fuses found archival footage from movies and current-affairs TV shows aimed at African Americans with a narrative about religious frenzy in the form of dance. Similarly emphasising the performative is Hannah Perry’s sculpture RAGE FLUIDS (2018), in which stretched, snaking, largescale coppery skins of car-body-wrap (vinyl film often used, by boy racers, to change the colour of a car without incurring the expense of a respray) vibrate according to the emissions of a series of subwoofers. Extending, perhaps, the exhibition’s earlier propositions of contingency when it comes to ‘Britishness’, to encompass a notion of animate rather than static form. Indeed, perhaps it’s only here that you truly get a suggestion of the form and function of the BAS coming together as one: that art might play an active role in life rather than simply offering a commentary on it. Which, one would hope, should be the ultimate goal of any edition of the BAS.

The British Art Show 10: A Chorus of Strangers is across various venues in Coventry, 2 October – 10 January

The artist’s ode to New York is strangely empty, and that’s probably the point

Jutta Koether’s exhibition cycles nimbly through several leitmotifs. These include her signature cartoon faces, which materialise, spooked and hollow-eyed, from bogs of spermlike tildes in paintings on the gallery’s ground floor like Soulpack (2000) and International Community: 3 from the heart of the brain (1997). Upstairs: a strange metallic square appears on canvases and cardboard, at times as a painted icon ( Homohomo 2 , 2002), at times as a scratched-up, tacked-on scrap of foil ( Metal Maniacs #2 , 2008). Spots and chequerboard patterns abound in the thumbtack-studded, tropophobia-inducing glazed black canvas Untitled (2007); a selection of dotted works of ink on paper in a vitrine; and paintings like Special purpose Entities I (2002), whose design resembles a red-and-white-gridded picnic blanket. Koether’s works here date from the mid-1990s, following the artist’s move from Germany to New York, to 2008, the year of the global financial crisis, making the show a time capsule of artistic production in the city, in a slightly more affordable, less gentrified and less automated era.

Koether came up in the then-male-dominated post-Neo-Expressionist Cologne art scene of the 1980s, where she became known early on for red and black paintings of fleshy forms and garrulous gestural marks. Red still appears throughout the paintings and mixed-media works at Buchholz, albeit relegated to accents, stains and outlines. Black makes up a more sizeable portion of the palette: chalkboardlike surfaces are inscribed and smudged with silver and gold ink or used as ground for wilder hues, as in the mixed-media piece The Mystical Sublime Stuff (2001), which boasts an off-centre patch of powdered-sugar white framed in sour purple.

Koether is also known for performing literary, musical and reportedly cringeworthy acts on her opening nights – not the case for this show (there wasn’t even a reception). However, two paintings on the gallery’s third floor, the final works one likely encounters in the exhibition, seem to pay homage to the performative aspect of her practice. One of these, titled Madison Square Garden and dated circa 1943 – which, per the press release, Koether bought at the Chelsea Flea Market – depicts varicoloured spotlights shining down on dancers in an arena. In the other – Koether’s reinterpretation of the scene on a canvas nearly three times as large, titled Dance at Madison Square Garden (1995) – the figures are absent, the light is stronger, fields of pigment curdle into scribbles and perspective is thrown askew.

Besides a name on the checklist, Fay Ruffo, we are told nothing about the artist behind the flea-market find, who is, safe to say, a far cry from any known quantity such as Nicolas Poussin, the French Baroque painter whose oeuvre Koether would later riff on, or William Blake and Walter Benjamin – who are referenced in this show via two oil paintings, WB II (William Blake / He Felt the female and C’) (1997) and WB IV (Walter Benjamin) (1997). And although the idea of shared or ambiguous authorship crops up often in Koether’s practice – she was, for instance, one of the brains behind the collectively written New York artworld novel Reena Spaulings (2005) – this pair of paintings doesn’t quite have the spirit of a collaboratively conceived diptych. Ruffo seems to be for Koether neither a revered forebearer nor an active interlocutor – or, it would seem, much of a subject of journalistic intrigue – but a figure Koether is performing for and performing on: with her inflated and deskilled rendition of Madison Square Garden , Koether seems to say, ‘I can do it better (ie worse) than you’, and thus to foist on this obscure person, who is essentially lost to art history, the very question that haunted the (1980s German) milieu from which she decamped: why paint?

The duelling canvases hang on adjacent walls, Koether’s on the left, Ruffo’s on the right, just as when they were displayed together in Painting – the extended field , an exhibition during the 1990s that proposed that the medium could renew itself by shapeshifting and commingling with other disciplines. Thirty years on and this pairing reappears as if it had stayed intact, frozen in time, while the world changed around it. Speaking to art historian Benjamin Buchloh in 2016, Koether called painting, as it seemed to her when she arrived in New York, an ‘abandoned building’ in which she was squatting. Perhaps this mood accounts for the lack of people in her Madison Square Garden; perhaps today the same can be said for the city itself.

Jutta Koether: Songs of New York at Galerie Buchholz, New York, 8 September – 31 October

article_text:
Sebastian Koch , star of Oscar-winning German film “The Lives of Others,” and Toni Servillo, protagonist of Italy’s Oscar winner “The Great Beauty,” are set to topline “The Lüneburg Variation,” a noir based in the world of chess, directed by Gabriele Salvatores .

Salvatores – himself also winner of an Oscar for “Mediterraneo” – has started shooting in Trieste on “Lüneburg Variation,” which is based on the eponymous novel by Italian author Paolo Maurensig that has been translated into 25 languages. Nine weeks of principal photography are planned between Trieste and Rome.

Related Stories

Jamie Dornan Says There's 'Pressure' to Taking Over Aragorn Role in 'Lord of the Rings: Hunt for Gollum': I'm Not 'Trying to Outdo' Viggo Mortensen

The film will be distributed in Italy by RAI Cinema’s 01 Distribution while RAI Cinema International Distribution is handling international sales.

The book opens with the suicide of a wealthy Munich businessman named Dieter Frisch near Vienna, leading to flashbacks of a revenge plot orchestrated through the game of chess.

“It is the story of a duel that lasts more than 40 years, fought by two adversaries on the battlefield of a chessboard. Chess! The most violent sport in existence and, perhaps, the least cinematic. It’s a great challenge, and one I was happy to take on,” Salvatores said in a statement.

The director added that he would delve into “the violent, magical, esoteric and mysterious dimension of chess, that is, instead, truly cinematic!”

“Maurensig envisioned a film of half-light; darkness and fire. Compelling and cruel. I hope I can deliver just that…,” Salvatores went on to note.

Rounding out the chess-world noir’s main cast are German actor Damian Hardung (“Maxton Hall”); Thomas Prenn, who is from South Tyrol and starred in Terrence Malick’s “A Hidden Life”; and Itay’s Eduardo Scarpetta (“My Brilliant Friend”).

“The Lüneburg Variation” is being lead-produced by Raffaella Leone and Andrea Leone through their Lotus Production, which is a Leone Film Group company, with RAI Cinema, in association with Vice Pictures and also in association with Italy’s Indiana, a Vuelta company, and MDE.

“We are very happy to be working with Gabriele Salvatores, a filmmaker and director we have always loved for the mastery with which he takes you by the hand and transports you into his world, making you fall in love with cinema all over again — real cinema, great cinema with a capital C,” Raffaella Leone said in a statement.

Francesco Melzi d’Eril, Leonardo Maria Del Vecchio, Riccardo Volpato, Marco Cohen, Benedetto Habib, Fabrizio Donvito and Daniel Campos Pavoncelli are also producers on the film, which is being supported by the Friuli Venezia Giulia Film Commission.

The key creative team on “Lüneburg Variation” comprises Diego Indraccolo as director of photography; Rita Rabassini as production designer; Patrizia Chericoni as costume designer; and Federico De Robertis as composer.

article_text:
そごう美術館（横浜市）で「KIRIKANE Sculpture 山本茜」が10月24日から12月6日まで開催されます。

1977年に石川県金沢市で生まれた山本茜は、京都市立芸術大学で日本画を学び、重要無形文化財「截金」保持者である江里佐代子氏のもとで伝統的截金技法を修得しました。その後、富山ガラス造形研究所でガラス技術の研鑽を積み、独自に「截金ガラス」という新たな表現領域を創り出しました。仏像や仏画の装飾技法として受け継がれてきた截金を、「装飾ではなく表現そのものとして空間に浮遊させたい」という思いから、透明なガラスを支持体とする独自の制作に挑戦。ガラス内部で截金が重なり合い交差する立体的な表現を実現し、「截金ガラス」は今もなお進化を続けています。

本展は、従来「截金ガラス」と称されてきた山本茜の作品を、新たに“KIRIKANE Sculpture”として発信する、美術館では初めての個展です。これまでの創作活動を集大成として振り返るとともに、KIRIKANE Sculptureという独創性と、新たな表現領域の可能性を示します。

KIRIKANE Sculpture 山本茜

会場：そごう美術館［横浜駅東口・そごう横浜店6階］（神奈川県横浜市西区高島2-18-1）

会期：2026年10月24日（土）～ 12月6日（日）

開館時間：10:00～20:00 ※入館は閉館の30分前まで

休館日：会期中無休

観覧料：一般2,000円、⼤学・高校⽣1,800円、中学生以下無料

詳しくは 公式サイト へ

“KIRIKANE Sculpture”に込めた想い

山本茜が生み出す、截金の精緻な美意識と重量感あるガラスを自在に操る造形力が融合した作品は、まさに「Sculpture（彫刻）」と言えます。そうした認識のもと、工芸という既存の枠組みを超えた立体表現として作品を捉え直し、これまでの歩みを礎に新たな創作へ踏み出してもらいたいという想いを込め、山本は自身の截金作品を“KIRIKANE Sculpture”と名付けました。

会場では、大学生時代の模写作品から木工に截金を施した作品を経て、独自の表現へと発展した截金ガラス作品までを展示し、作家活動の軌跡をたどります。また、初めて手がけた截金ガラス作品から最新作までを一堂に紹介し、常に技術と表現の革新に挑み続ける創作の変遷を約60点の作品からたどります。さらに、ライフワークとして取り組む『源氏物語』シリーズを可能な限り集め、それぞれの場面に込められた物語世界と造形表現の広がりを紹介します。あわせて、創作の原点ともいえる工房空間を再現することで、作品が生まれる現場の息づかいや制作工程にも触れることができる構成となっています。

最新作《源氏物語シリーズ第十八帖「松風」―浮木舟―》初公開

中学生のころに出逢った『源氏物語』は山本茜の創作の原点になりました。2010年から『源氏物語』全五十四帖を独自の解釈で表現することをライフワークとして取り組み続けています。本展覧会では、シリーズ24作目となる《源氏物語シリーズ第十八帖「松風」―浮木舟―》を初公開。4年の歳月をかけて完成した本作からも、いまなお進化を続ける山本茜の『源氏物語』を捉えた独自の世界を見ることができます。

──いくかへり行きかふ秋を過ぐしつつ 浮木に乗りてわれ帰るらむ

明石の御方が源氏の求めに応じて上洛する際、舟の上で詠んだ歌です。「浮木」という言葉に、故郷を離れる明石の御方の不安な気持ちが凝縮されているようで、丸太のような、舟のような形状のガラスの中に、彼女の不安で波立つ心を折り重なる截金の波で表現しています。山本は、舟上で耳にしたであろう波の音と、故郷の明石の松と、移り住んだ大堰の松の葉ずれの音が聴こえるような作品を目指し、何度も明石の浦から大堰川（嵐山）を往復して、明石の御方の旅情に心を重ね、松や波をスケッチして截金文様に落とし込んだといいます。

15ピースのガラスを、融着して一体にするという規格外の難題に挑戦した作品です。完成までに通算52回の窯入れと4年の歳月を費やした渾身の作を、ぜひ会場で味わってみてください。

主な展示作品
